item.title: @SemiconductorsX：SK海力士计划在4到5年内实现100层3D DRAM量产，预计2031年左右实现商业化
item.description:
SK Hynix targets first 3D DRAM at 100 layers. Mass production is set for 4 to 5 years.

Choi Kang-sik, a distinguished engineer, said on the 25th at the Seoul National University AI Semiconductor Forum that the company is developing 3D DRAM with volume production in mind within that window. Commercialization is expected around 2031. Matching current 10-nm-class density needs about 75 layers. Extra factors push the first product to start at 100 layers.
$SKHY
Current equipment can handle that layer count. 200 to 300 layers and above will need dedicated tools. Longer term, the company is looking at multi-stacking and hybrid bonding used in 3D NAND to reach beyond 1,000 layers. It has already built 3D DRAM cells and verified operation. Refresh characteristics match existing DRAM.

3D DRAM stacks memory cells vertically. It is different from HBM or logic-on-DRAM stacking. The shift comes as planar scaling hits limits. Smaller cells hold less charge and raise leakage and resistance. Stacking upward solves the charge problem and lifts density.

The structure uses layered silicon and silicon-germanium that are etched. Higher layer counts make connections more complex and etching harder. SK Hynix is studying a selector structure that activates only needed circuits to cut area and electrical load. Cost reduction looks at etch process integration from 3D NAND.

It is also researching a switch from silicon to IGZO for the transistor channel. IGZO has lower leakage and can extend data retention. Hydrogen sensitivity remains a challenge. Choi said reliable IGZO could become a game changer for 3D DRAM.

How much of the 100-layer first product stays on current tools once the 4-to-5-year production window starts?

“Some major substrate manufacturers are even making advance payments to equipment suppliers to speed up delivery,” an industry source said. “The equipment still takes a long time to arrive, and only a limited number of substrate makers have secured supply.”

Equipment makers stand to benefit from the surge in AI investment, but they’re struggling to keep up with orders. The biggest bottleneck is securing components. The more advanced the equipment, the more it relies on Japanese-made parts, and Japanese component suppliers have limited production capacity.

“Japanese parts we could normally get right away now take about six months to arrive,” said the head of an FC-BGA bonding equipment maker. “If we can’t stock up on these parts ahead of time, production of FC-BGA equipment could be disrupted.”

Samsung hit 17Gbps per pin on HBM4E. That is up from the 16Gbps max it showed in May, six months earlier.

The company will present a 48GB HBM4E running at 17Gbps at ISSCC 2027 in San Francisco next February. The paper from Hwaseong researchers is already listed for February 16. It moves into the 17-18Gbps range that has been tied to Nvidia’s request. Samsung is known to have targeted that band on an 8-hi HBM4E. The paper does not confirm whether this 48GB stack is the same as the Nvidia 8-hi version. Samsung earlier described its 48GB part as 12-hi and said it would add 32GB 8-hi and 64GB 16-hi versions.

On a 2048-bit interface, 17Gbps gives a theoretical peak bandwidth of 4.35 TB/s. That is about 0.26 TB/s above the 4.10 TB/s figure at 16Gbps. The paper also covers an eye monitor for signal quality and voltage-drop detection so stability can be checked at the wafer stage.

The speed and bandwidth gains matter for AI accelerators. HBM4E is expected to be the next focus of the three-way race with SK Hynix and Micron.

item.title: 【回复】@mitchellh：讨论libghostty在社区中的广泛嵌入与用户基础
item.description:
被回答的问题 @JonofFive
@mitchellh How are you surfacing these bugs? They feel obscure yet there's a broad range of them. AI assisted testing?
原帖

回复 @mitchellh
libghostty-vt 1.0.2 released: correct widths for skin tone emoji, insert/delete line (IL/DL) fixes, up to 1.8x faster scrolling inside left/right margins (think tmux side-by-side panes or Neovim vertical splits), and more. Release notes below.

https://lib.ghostty.org/vt/release-notes.html

Bug Fixes:

- The mouse encoder no longer forgets the last cell when calling `ghostty_mouse_encoder_set_from_terminal` and setting the size now only forget it when the value actually changes. Previously, with `GHOSTTY_MOUSE_ENCODER_OPT_TRACK_LAST_CELL` on, motion in the same cell was reported again, so a click could come out as a press, a motion and a release. This isn't incorrect VT sequencing, but it was wasteful and unnecessary.
- With grapheme clustering (mode 2027), a skin tone modifier now makes an emoji that is text by default 2 cells wide, the same as VS16. For example, U+261D U+1F3FB (index pointing up, light skin tone) was 1 cell and is now 2. `ghostty_unicode_grapheme_width` changes the same way.
- Terminals created with the C API now ignore the Kitty drag and drop protocol (OSC 72), including its queries. The C API can't deliver drops yet, so programs registered for drops that never came instead of falling back.
- Insert and delete lines (IL and DL) no longer break the soft wraps of rows that move together. Previously a wrapped line in the scroll region, such as a long URL, became two lines until the program redrew it.
- Insert and delete lines with left and right margins no longer drop the semantic prompt marks (OSC 133) of the rows they move, so scrolling by prompts no longer skips prompts.
- Kitty graphics: Unicode placeholders no longer disappear when insert or delete lines with left and right margins move their row.
- A restored snapshot now keeps a pending wrap at any column, for both the cursor and the saved cursor (DECSC). Previously it was kept only on the last column, so with a right margin (DECSLRM) the next character overwrote the cursor cell instead of wrapping. The snapshot format is unchanged.

Performance:

- Insert and delete lines with left and right margins now move styled rows with a single copy. This is how tmux scrolls a pane next to another pane, and how Neovim scrolls a vertical split. A stream that does this went from 1,716 to 936 ms on x86_64 (1.8x) and from 1,100 to 695 ms on an M1 Pro (1.6x).
- Hyperlinks (OSC 8) are hashed in one pass instead of a byte at a time. `ls -laR --hyperlink=always` output is 1.3x faster.
- Carriage returns and absolute column moves (CHA, HPA) no longer look up the cursor's row again. Scrolling streams are up to 6% faster.
- Erasing cells skips rows that are already blank and releases styles a run at a time instead of a cell at a time. Erase-heavy streams are 3–6% faster.

item.description:
被回答的问题 @chevlume
@chris_j_paxton @XSquareRobot How is the 55.1% scored: one binary trial per task, or several trials with partial credit for subtasks? With 312 one-off tasks, per-task variance could matter as much as the mean.
原帖

回复 @chris_j_paxton
I really like the way @XSquareRobot evaluated this model. Letting evaluators choose the tasks makes it a really nice measure of generality; 312 different tasks chosen by evaluators is impressive. And 55.1% may not sound like a lot but on a wide range of tasks I think there’s little comparison.

And the harness is interesting. We’re approaching the period in robotics where the harness is going to be really important. The harness gives this information to an extra watcher which will do things like determine if conditions are met to execute the next step in the task.

Say I want to pick up a pen and remove its cap. The watcher says the pen’s in hand, and when it can advance to the next stage. It’s an interesting idea and progress toward reliability and error recovery that will be crucial for deploying all these zero-shot capabilities on robots in the real world. I’d love to see how it works on real tasks with and without this watcher.
